newsitem.title: USA: Cohen urges bipartisan U.S. military policy.
newsitem.headline: Cohen urges bipartisan U.S. military policy.

text.p: Defence Secretary nominee William Cohen urged the Republican-led Congress on Wednesday to give President Bill Clinton bipartisan support for continued U.S. leadership in the world.

The retired Republican senator from Maine also promised to give personal emphasis to Asia and the Pacific. "I intend to give new focus to our security relations in the Asia-Pacific region," told the Senate Armed Services Committee at the opening of his confirmation hearing.

Cohen, 56, was expected to be confirmed rapidly by the Senate as the first Republican in Clinton's Cabinet, said his nomination was "a clear signal" of the president's commitment to the principle that U.S. security was not a partisan matter.

Republicans in Congress have complained that U.S. defence budgets have been cut too deeply after the Cold War. Cohen promised to fight further cuts, saying he would never "paper over" differences he might have with the White House.

Cohen, who would replace William Perry, said any personal differences with Clinton would be settled behind closed doors. He stressed that bipartisanship was necessary to deal with Russia and other emerging democracies in Europe as well as tensions in East Asia and Southwest Asia.

"As the centre of gravity of the world economy has shifted to the Pacific, our increasing economic integration with Asia's dynamic economies has created enormous opportunities for American businessmen and workers," he testified.
The United States is worried about continued friction between India and Pakistan and is seeking to forge closer ties with China despite differences over human rights and trade.
Cohen, who retired this month after 24 years in Congress, was repeatedly praised by Republican and Democratic senators as a moderate consensus-builder.
"While there always will be room for legitimate debate on national security issues, partisanship and parochialism should occupy no seat at the table of our deliberations," he said.

Despite calls from many Republicans for an agreement to deploy a national missile defence by 2003, he said he agreed with the administration plan to do so only if developments in the world warrant the costly "Starwars" programme.

Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters on Tuesday that Cohen, who served on both the armed services and intelligence committees in the Senate, would devote early weeks on the job to the fiscal 1998 defence budget and to a major quadrennial review of U.S. defence policy.
After presenting the budget to Congress in hearings early next month, Cohen is likely to begin travelling to visit U.S. troops and other defence ministers, Bacon said.

Among challenges he will face are a U.S. push to develop closer military ties with China while standing firm on human rights and trade issues and forging better ties with Russia despite Moscow's opposition to NATO enlargement into Eastern and Central Europe.
